blocks.text: The reactivity of alkenes follows from the structure of the carbon-carbon double bond. This section describes the structure of ethene (11.7.1), the reactivity of the pi bond, carbocation stability and the inductive effect of alkyl groups (11.7.2) and the electron-withdrawing inductive effect (11.7.3). Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes, and their reactions mostly proceed through carbocations.

blocks.prompt: How does an alkane differ from an alkene in stability (Quick Check 11.5a)?
blocks.explanation: An alkane has only strong sigma bonds and is stable towards most reagents; an alkene has in addition a pi bond whose electrons lie above and below the bond axis, are held loosely and are easily attacked by electrophiles, so the alkene is less stable and far more reactive.

items: Alkene reactivity comes from the C=C structure: a weak, exposed pi bond and reactions through carbocations (11.7.1 to 11.7.3).
